newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung likely to name top officials this month.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung likely to name top officials this month.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa said on Tuesday he expected to name the top officials of his administration by the end of this month.

"I will release the names and my recommendations and my decisions probably towards the end of January because that would be the time when I complete the process of interviews," Tung told reporters on Tuesday.
Tung said he sought "people with commitment to Hong Kong, very experienced and capable, good leaders, good communicators, and of course the residential qualifications needed under the Basic Law".
Under the Basic Law, Hong Kong's China-drawn future constitution, top officials may not have right of residence abroad, and several officials have given up foreign passports.

Tung, chief executive-designate of the government that will take over Hong Kong after the British colony reverts to Chinese sovereignty at midnight of June 30, has been interviewing all principal officials of the current administration.
So far, only Chief Secretary Anson Chan, governor Chris Patten's number two, has been asked to stay on.
Tung also hinted he might visit Washington in the near future to try to ease doubts there about Hong Kong's future as a part of China.

"It was suggested it would be helpful if I visited Washington earlier to explain the current development in Hong Kong. It was a very good suggestion and I would certainly take that into account in my planning," he said.

Tung said he wanted to explain that people in Hong Kong were confident, and that China's promise to allow Hong Kong to keep its capitalist system and run its own affairs for 50 years after the handover would be kept.

"I (want) to explain to Washington what is happening here in Hong Kong and that there is a high degree of confidence here, and that 'one-country two-systems' and 'a high degree of autonomy' will prevail," he said.
Tung's aides said last weekend that he was making plans to travel to major Western countries in a bid to raise Hong Kong's profile and clear the air over the transition of sovereignty.
